name: Chromium
summary: A multi-process browser engine that isolates browser services and web content, turns Blink document work into composited output, and connects privileged services through Mojo while applying sandbox and failure boundaries.

features.name: Browser, renderer, and service process isolation
features.description: Chromium separates browser coordination from renderer execution and uses additional processes for selected services. The process model makes web content a failure and privilege boundary rather than an in-process browser extension.
benefits: Limits compromised or crashed web content to a process boundary
Allows browser-owned services and renderers to evolve independently
costs: Process startup, memory, and cross-process coordination add overhead
A feature must define which process owns authority and lifecycle

features.name: Blink document parsing, layout, and compositor pipeline
features.description: Blink source contains distinct parser, layout, paint, and compositing stages that transform web input into a renderable layer tree. The renderer process coordinates these stages while compositor code consumes derived rendering state.
benefits: Separates document interpretation from geometry and display scheduling
Provides derived rendering state that can be composited independently
costs: Invalidation and synchronization across stages make rendering state complex
Layout, paint, and compositor work can consume substantial CPU and memory

features.name: Mojo interface-mediated IPC
features.description: Chromium uses Mojo interfaces and message pipes to define typed asynchronous communication between processes and services. Browser and renderer code bind interfaces to task-runner-owned implementations rather than sharing arbitrary process memory.
benefits: Makes authority and communication contracts explicit at service boundaries
Supports asynchronous calls and independently hosted implementations
costs: Interface versioning, serialization, and disconnect handling become protocol obligations
Cross-process calls add latency and failure states

features.name: Partitioned network and storage services
features.description: Chromium centralizes network and browser storage behind browser-side service and partition boundaries. Network requests and storage access are associated with browser contexts such as profiles, storage partitions, and site data rather than being unrestricted renderer capabilities.
benefits: Centralizes policy, caching, persistence, and network authority
Allows site or profile boundaries to constrain state sharing
costs: Partition keys and service ownership complicate cache and storage behavior
Renderer-to-service round trips affect latency and lifecycle handling

features.name: Sandboxed process and failure boundaries
features.description: Chromium applies sandbox restrictions to processes handling less-trusted content and treats process launch, IPC disconnection, crash, and restart as explicit lifecycle conditions. The sandbox reduces direct operating-system authority but requires brokered access through trusted processes.
benefits: Reduces the authority available after a renderer or service compromise
Contains selected crashes and allows the browser to observe process loss
costs: Brokered operations and sandbox policy maintenance add implementation complexity
A process failure can invalidate in-flight requests and derived rendering state

mathematical_views.question: Which browser, renderer, and service processes may communicate, and which authority is available across each boundary?
assumptions: Processes are nodes and Mojo interfaces are labeled communication edges
Sandbox policy is modeled as an authority restriction on process nodes
The graph abstracts operating-system scheduler details and implementation-specific broker rules

mathematical_views.question: How do parser, style, layout, paint, and compositor transitions transform document input into displayable output?
assumptions: Each stage consumes a representation produced by an earlier stage
Invalidation and scheduling are represented as labeled transitions
GPU driver behavior and pixel-level equivalence are outside the model

mathematical_views.question: How do profiles, sites, storage partitions, network contexts, and renderer requests determine state ownership and sharing?
assumptions: Partition keys label resource and service ownership edges
A renderer request is an input to a browser-owned service rather than direct storage authority
The view does not claim that partitioning alone proves complete privacy isolation

benefits: Fault and privilege separation for web content
Centralized policy and constrained state sharing
Reduced post-compromise authority and contained failures
